It feels so obvious and disgusting to me that I can’t understand how others don’t see it.

D021-D005_h023.question_both:
I guess the main reason I’m here is that my eating has gotten…strange, I guess, over the last six or seven months. I track everything I eat down to the gram and try to keep it as low as possible. If I go over what I’ve set for the day, I feel really guilty and anxious, like I’ve messed up something important. I weigh myself multiple times a day, sometimes even between Zoom meetings, and if the number is even slightly higher I panic and start planning how to cut more the next day.

My husband and my PCP keep saying I’m “too thin” and need to gain weight, but I honestly don’t see what the big medical issue is. I still get my work done, I still run my analyses, so I feel like they’re making it sound worse than it actually is.

At the same time, I’ve had this persistent feeling that something is “off” about food in general. It’s hard to explain—like certain foods might not be what they seem, or they could somehow interfere with my thinking or my research if I’m not careful. I know that probably sounds odd, but it’s been in the back of my mind for a while and it definitely affects what I’m willing to eat.
D021-D005_h023.question_a:
I’m a computational biologist, so I think a lot in numbers, and lately my whole life revolves around numbers tied to food and my weight. For about the past year, I’ve been cutting my intake down more and more—now I won’t let myself go over about 600–700 calories a day, and most days I try to stay under that. I track everything obsessively in an app and on spreadsheets.

I weigh myself multiple times a day. If the scale goes up even 0.2 kilos, I panic. I’ll skip the next meal, add more time on the treadmill, or drink extra coffee to “fix” it. My husband keeps saying I’m “too thin,” but when I look in the mirror, I still see fat on my stomach and thighs. It feels like if I eat normally, I’ll just blow up overnight. That thought feels so real it’s almost like a fact, not something you could argue me out of.

My GP has mentioned my labs are off and that I’m underweight, but I don’t really see it as dangerous—people diet all the time. I feel like they’re overreacting.
D021-D005_h023.question_b:
I’ve lost quite a bit of weight over the past few months, but it’s not really about how I look or being afraid of getting fat. Food has just become… complicated. Some days I’m convinced certain foods are “contaminated” in a way other people can’t detect, or that if I eat something specific it might interfere with the signals I think are being sent to me. So I end up eating very little, almost like I’m rationing for safety, not for my figure.

My husband keeps pointing out how thin I’ve gotten and that I’m barely getting any calories, but I don’t feel like I’m in danger physically. I’m more worried about what I feel is happening around me—like I’m being watched or monitored, even at work. Sometimes I hear a voice commenting on what I’m doing, including when I’m eating, even when no one’s there. That’s part of why I avoid meals with colleagues. This has been going on for at least six months, gradually getting worse, and my work as a scientist is suffering because I can’t trust my own perceptions.

I guess this started maybe a few months ago. I just don’t feel like eating much. Most days I’ll “forget” breakfast and then tell myself I’ll just have a cup of tea for lunch. By dinner I’m not really hungry, so I’ll pick at a bit of toast or fruit and call it enough. I could cook more, but I usually decide it’s better not to.

I get nervous around certain foods now, especially things that seem heavy or rich. It sounds silly, but I feel like if I eat something like that, it’ll just sit on me and I’ll put on weight straight away, even though people say I’ve thinned out. So I avoid them and stick to what feels “safe.”

My daughter worries because I get light‑headed when I stand up and I’ve noticed more hair in the sink, but I keep telling her it’s just old age and not worth making a fuss about.

Sometimes I get this strong sense that something in the food isn’t right, like it’s been tampered with or will do something bad to me, even when I know that doesn’t quite make sense. It makes it even harder to eat.
D021-D005_h024.question_a:
It’s been going on maybe… a year? A bit more. Since my wife died, really. I’ve been cutting back on what I eat. At first it was just smaller portions, but now I’ll “forget” breakfast, pick at lunch, and tell my daughter I’m not hungry at dinner. Truth is, I’m doing it on purpose. I’m terrified that if I eat a proper meal, especially anything heavy—bread, potatoes, dessert—it’ll go straight to my belly and I’ll blow up overnight. 

I know I’m old and everyone keeps saying I’m “too thin,” but when I look in the mirror, I still see this soft gut and flabby arms. My trousers feel loose but I can’t shake the idea that I’m one big meal away from getting fat and useless, needing help with everything. Sometimes I get dizzy when I stand, and my hair’s been coming out in the shower, but I just tell myself it’s normal for my age and not worth fussing over. 

My son worries I’m “wasting away,” but I’m more afraid of becoming a burden, heavy and helpless. So I just keep skipping meals.
D021-D005_h024.question_b:
I’ve lost quite a bit of weight over the past year, maybe more than 10 kilos, but it wasn’t because I’m trying to be thinner or anything like that. I’m 80, I don’t care about my figure. It’s more that I just… don’t trust the food sometimes. I’ll skip meals because I feel like something is wrong with it, like it’s been tampered with, or that people are trying to poison me. My daughter brings groceries and says everything is fine, but I’m not convinced, so I might just have tea and a biscuit instead of a proper dinner.

This has been going on for at least a year, getting worse in the last several months. I get dizzy sometimes when I stand up, but I just push through it. What bothers me most is this feeling that the neighbors are talking about me through the walls, and that the TV is sending me hidden messages. I know that sounds odd, but it feels very real. The eating and weight loss are sort of wrapped up in that—more about suspicion and these ideas than any fear of getting fat.
